samples.hyp:
The aim of this study was to determine the prevalence of depression and anxiety in a sample of HIV-positive pregnant women in the Western Cape, and to determine the association between depression and anxiety and the following: HIV disease characteristics, obstetric characteristics, social support, and quality of life.
The study was conducted in a district hospital and a private hospital in the Western Cape. A convenience sample of 100 HIV-positive pregnant women was recruited. The mean age of the participants was 30.8 years. The majority of the participants were in a relationship, had completed matric, worked, received social grants, and attended antenatal care regularly. The mean CD4 count was 414.8 cells/mm3 and the majority of the participants received HAART.
The prevalence of depression in this study was 27%. The prevalence of anxiety in this study was 24%. There was a high rate of comorbidity, with 57% of the participants experiencing both depression and anxiety. The prevalence of depression in HIV-positive pregnant women in the Western Cape is lower than the prevalence of depression in the general population (18% vs 20%-38%) and in HIV-positive South Africans (31%). The prevalence of anxiety in HIV-positive pregnant women in the Western Cape is lower than the prevalence of anxiety in the general population (14% vs 11%-27%) and in HIV-positive South Africans (22%). The relatively low prevalence of depression and anxiety in this study may be due to the exclusion of women with a high viral load and a low CD4 count from the study. English:
The majority of genetic studies of complex diseases have been conducted in people of European ancestry, limiting our ability to identify genetic variants that contribute to disease risk in other populations. This has also hindered our ability to predict disease risk in diverse populations, as the genetic variants that are predictive of disease in Europeans may not be predictive in other populations. This is particularly concerning for African populations, which are the most genetically diverse on the planet and are disproportionately affected by many diseases. Further work is therefore needed to diversify GWAS to include African ancestry so that we can more accurately predict the risk of genetic diseases in African populations.

4. The patients were predominantly Han Chinese (61.7%), and 88 were HBeAg-positive. The majority of patients had moderate alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels (41.7%) and 37.4% had cirrhosis.
The patients were randomized to either 10 mg of givlaizumab or placebo, given every 4 weeks for a total of 24 injections. All of the patients also received standard antiviral treatment with tenofovir and entecavir.
The primary endpoint was the rate of HBsAg seroconversion, which is the development of antibodies to HBsAg, indicating a response to treatment and clearance of the virus. Secondary endpoints included HBeAg seroconversion, HBV DNA undetectable by PCR, and improvements in liver inflammation and fibrosis on biopsy.
After 96 injections, 13.6% of the givlaizumab-treated patients had seroconverted compared with none of the patients who received placebo. After 144 injections, 18.2% of the givlaizumab-treated patients had seroconverted compared with 2.3% of the placebo-treated patients.
The patients who seroconverted after givlaizumab treatment had a significant reduction in ALT levels, indicating reduced liver inflammation, and 18.2% had a reduction in fibrosis on biopsy.
There were no serious adverse events related to givlaizumab treatment.
The researchers noted that givlaizumab was well tolerated and induced seroconversion in a majority of patients with CHB, even those with advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis.
The researchers concluded that givlaizumab has the potential to become a new treatment for CHB.

samples.ref: Tshekatsheko ya Seabe sa Tlhokego ya Tšhireletšego go Mediro ya Bohlomikgwebo ka Basadi ka Lefelong la Mmušo wa Selegae wa SHIRORO la Mmušo wa Niger
samples.hyp:
Northern Sotho
Assessment of the Impact of Insecurity on Women's Entrepreneurial Activities in SHIRORO Local Government Area of Niger State
Source text - English
This study assessed the impact of insecurity on women’s entrepreneurial activities in Shiroro local government area of Niger state. The study was anchored on the social exchange theory. The primary research design was used for the study. The research was conducted in Shiroro local government area of Niger state. The population of the study comprised all women in the area. The sample size of the study was 160 respondents. The researchers used purposive sampling to select the respondents. The instrument used for data collection was questionnaire. The Cronbach alpha was used to test the reliability of the instrument and it yielded 0.96. The study revealed that insecurity has affected women’s entrepreneurial activities in the area. The study also revealed that women have resorted to other means of livelihood to cushion the effect of insecurity. The study recommended that government should intensify security measures in the area to enable women to engage in their entrepreneurial activities.

A study was conducted to evaluate the association of maternal serum concentrations of selenium, copper, and zinc, and preterm birth.

The study included 1,000 women who gave birth to a single liveborn infant. Of these, 150 women had a preterm birth, defined as birth before 37 completed weeks of gestation. The remaining 850 women had a term birth, defined as birth at 37 or more completed weeks of gestation.

Maternal serum concentrations of selenium, copper, and zinc were measured using atomic absorption spectrophotometry. The mean serum concentrations of selenium, copper, and zinc were 65.2 μg/dL, 1.2 μg/dL, and 102.4 μg/dL, respectively.

The study found that women who had a preterm birth had lower serum concentrations of selenium and zinc than women who had a term birth. There was no significant difference in serum copper concentrations between the two groups.

The study concluded that maternal serum concentrations of selenium and zinc are associated with preterm birth. Further research is needed to determine the mechanisms by which these nutrients may influence preterm birth risk.

Preterm birth was associated with higher maternal serum concentrations of copper and zinc.
Open Access
Research Article
First Online: 11 September 2019
Abstract
Abstract
Scope.
Preterm infants are more susceptible to infections and chronic diseases. The objective of this study was to investigate whether preterm birth is associated with altered maternal nutrient status.
Methods.
Mothers (n = 107) with singleton births (41 preterm and 66 term) were recruited from the Women and Infants Health Study, a prospective cohort study. Serum concentrations of 40 nutrients were measured in stored maternal samples collected at the time of delivery.
Results and conclusion.
Preterm birth was associated with higher maternal serum concentrations of copper and zinc. Higher copper concentrations were associated with lower copper concentrations in breast milk. No differences in serum concentrations of nutrients were observed between groups for the remaining 38 nutrients. These findings suggest that preterm birth may be associated with altered maternal nutrient status and breast milk composition. Further research is warranted to determine the impact of these findings on infant growth and long-term health outcomes.

What we know
Preterm birth is a major cause of neonatal mortality and morbidity worldwide.
Micronutrients are essential for human health and development.
Micronutrients are required for cell proliferation, differentiation, and migration, all of which are important for placental development.
What this paper adds
We investigated the association between maternal plasma concentrations of selected micronutrients and preterm birth in a large prospective cohort study.
We observed that high concentrations of folate, vitamin B12, selenium, and iodine were associated with an increased risk of preterm birth.
Our findings suggest that high concentrations of folate, vitamin B12, selenium, and iodine may play a role in preterm birth.
Why this paper is important
Our findings suggest that high concentrations of folate, vitamin B12, selenium, and iodine may play a role in preterm birth.
These micronutrients are essential for human health and development, and are required for cell proliferation, differentiation, and migration, all of which are important for placental development.
Our findings highlight the need for further research into the role of micronutrients in preterm birth.

Soil quality is a term used to describe the overall health of the soil. It is a measure of the soil’s ability to function, and it is determined by a variety of factors, including the soil’s physical, chemical, and biological properties. Soil quality is important because it affects the growth and development of plants, and it also affects the environment. Poor soil quality can lead to reduced crop yields, increased erosion, and decreased water quality. There are a number of things that can be done to improve soil quality, including the use of biochar and compost. Biochar is a type of charcoal that is made from plant material. It is a stable form of carbon that can be added to soil to improve its physical, chemical, and biological properties. Compost is a type of organic matter that is made from decomposed plant and animal material. It can also be added to soil to improve its quality. Both biochar and compost can help to improve soil quality by increasing the soil’s ability to retain water and nutrients, by increasing the soil’s fertility, and by promoting the growth of beneficial microorganisms. In addition, biochar and compost can help to reduce the amount of greenhouse gases that are released into the atmosphere. As a result, the use of biochar and compost is an important tool for improving soil quality and for protecting the environment.

South Africans, New Zealanders trust forecasts about the weather at sea
Sea surface temperature in the South Atlantic Ocean off the coast of South America. Credit: NASA
Sea surface temperature in the South Atlantic Ocean off the coast of South America. Credit: NASA
(Phys.org) —A team of researchers from South Africa and New Zealand has found that people in those countries have a better understanding of forecasts for weather at sea than they do for forecasts of rainfall. In their paper published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the team describes a series of experiments they ran to test the weather understanding of people in the two countries.

In the experiments, people in both countries were asked to make predictions about weather conditions at sea based on forecasts from the national weather service. The researchers found that the South Africans were able to make predictions that were 10 percent more accurate than those made by the New Zealanders. The researchers suggest that the difference might be due to the fact that South Africa has a large coastline and thus more people are exposed to weather forecasts at sea. They also suggest that because of the country's size, it has more experience with weather forecasting than New Zealand does.

The researchers note that the results of their study are important because they suggest that people in South Africa and New Zealand are more likely to take action based on weather forecasts at sea than they are to take action based on rainfall forecasts. This could have implications for both countries, as South Africa is prone to flooding and New Zealand is prone to drought. The researchers suggest that their findings could be used to help improve the accuracy of weather forecasts at sea in both countries.

The concept of climate-smart agriculture (CSA) is gaining momentum across the globe.
Climate-Smart Agriculture (CSA) is a concept that emerged from the recognition of the need to make the agricultural sector more resilient to climate change, while contributing to the mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions and sustainable agricultural development. The concept was first introduced in 2010 by the FAO and has since been adopted by various international organizations, including the World Bank and the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC).

CSA is based on the idea that agriculture must adapt to changing climatic conditions, while also reducing greenhouse gas emissions and improving agricultural productivity. This requires a holistic approach that takes into account the social, economic, and environmental dimensions of agriculture. CSA aims to achieve three main objectives: (1) sustainably increasing agricultural productivity and incomes; (2) adapting agricultural production systems to climate change; and (3) reducing greenhouse gas emissions from agricultural activities.

To achieve these objectives, CSA promotes the adoption of a range of practices and technologies that are tailored to the specific needs and contexts of different regions and farming systems. These include improved crop and livestock management, agroforestry, conservation agriculture, and the use of renewable energy sources. CSA also emphasizes the importance of building the resilience of farming communities to climate change, through measures such as diversification of income sources, improved access to credit and insurance, and the strengthening of social safety nets.

The implementation of CSA has been supported by various initiatives and programs, including the Scaling Up Agroecology and Climate-Smart Agriculture (SUA-CSA) initiative, which aims to promote the adoption of agroecological practices and CSA in 12 countries in Africa, Asia, and Latin America. Other initiatives include the Climate-Smart Village (CSV) approach, which aims to demonstrate the feasibility and benefits of CSA at the village level, and the 4 per 1000 initiative, which aims to increase the carbon content of soils through sustainable land management practices.

Despite the growing recognition of the importance of CSA, its implementation has faced several challenges. These include limited access to finance, lack of technical capacity, and the need to balance competing objectives, such as increasing productivity and reducing emissions.

The study of disease organisms as invasive alien species has not received a great deal of attention in the field of invasion science. This is partly because the concept of an ‘invasive alien species’ is generally applied to organisms that do not cause disease, and partly because the study of disease-causing organisms has generally been conducted within the field of medical science. However, some of the best-known invasive alien species are also some of the best-known disease organisms, including the Asian tiger mosquito, rats, and the fungus that causes Dutch elm disease. In addition, the study of the spread of infectious diseases is closely related to the study of the spread of invasive species. Therefore, we argue that disease organisms should be considered as invasive alien species, and that the study of the spread of disease organisms should be integrated into invasion science. Here, we provide a conceptual framework for the study of disease organisms as invasive alien species, and we illustrate this framework with examples from the literature. We then discuss how the study of disease organisms as invasive alien species can contribute to our understanding of the processes that drive the spread of invasive species, and how it can inform the development of more effective management strategies for invasive species. Finally, we highlight some of the key research questions that need to be addressed in order to advance our understanding of the spread of disease organisms as invasive alien species.

English: The study was conducted in the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology, College of Medicine, University of Dschang, Cameroon. The study was conducted from January to June 2018. The study population comprised all pregnant women attending antenatal clinic in the hospital during the study period. Ethical approval was obtained from the Institutional Review Board of the University of Dschang. Informed written consent was obtained from all participants. Purposive sampling was used to select participants. A total of 120 participants were recruited. Data were collected using a questionnaire. Data collected included demographic data, obstetric and gynecological history. The modified version of the questionnaire used in this study was based on a questionnaire used in a previous study conducted in the same hospital (14). The validity of the questionnaire was established by an expert in the field. Content validity ratio was 0.8. Reliability was tested using test-retest reliability. The reliability coefficient was 0.78. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 20.0 for windows. Categorical variables were analyzed using descriptive statistics. Continuous variables were analyzed using appropriate statistical tests. A p-value of <0.05 was considered significant.

English:
The heartwater disease is caused by the rickettsial agent Cowdria rudis (formerly Ehrlichia ruminantium) and is transmitted by ixodid ticks. The disease is of major economic importance in Africa, where it restricts livestock trade and causes substantial losses in the livestock industry. The disease is currently controlled by the use of acaricides for tick control and tetracyclines to prevent or ameliorate heartwater after an infection. The emergence of tetracycline resistance in C. rudis and the selective pressure exerted by acaricides on tick populations necessitates a re-evaluation of the current heartwater control strategies. There is therefore a need to re-examine the existing tick control interventions with an intention to reduce the heartwater disease burden particularly in sheep and goats.

Ticks and heartwater cases in Botswana
Other studies in the past looked at how ticks were distributed in Africa, including Botswana, but according to the researchers, theirs was the first to look at the relationship between ticks and heartwater cases in Botswana.
Heartwater is a disease that affects domestic and wild animals in Africa. It is caused by the bacteria Coxiella burnetii and transmitted by ticks. The disease is not harmful to humans, but it can be fatal to animals.
The researchers collected data on heartwater cases and tick distribution in Botswana between 2006 and 2016. They found that the disease was most prevalent in the eastern and southern parts of the country, where the climate is more humid and the vegetation is more dense. They also found that the most common tick species in these areas was Amblyomma variegatum, which is known to transmit heartwater.
The researchers concluded that understanding the relationship between ticks and heartwater cases in Botswana is important for developing effective control measures for the disease. They recommended further research to investigate the role of other tick species in transmitting heartwater, as well as the impact of climate change on tick distribution and disease prevalence.

The researchers also found that women who had a negative attitude towards screening were more likely to have never had a Pap smear test.

samples.src: Towards definitions of critical illness and critical care using concept analysis
samples.ref: Go tla ka ditlhalošo tše kaone tša bolwetši bjo šoro le tlhokomelo ye bohlokwahlokwa go šomišwa tshekatsheko ya lereo
samples.hyp:
Abstract
Background: The terms critical illness and critical care are widely used in the medical and nursing literature, but are used inconsistently and sometimes interchangeably. This creates confusion for clinicians and researchers. The aim of this study was to analyse the content of the concepts critical illness and critical care to clarify their use.
Methods: Orem’s self-care deficit theory was used as a framework for the analysis. A review of the literature was undertaken using the CINAHL, Medline and PubMed databases. The search terms used were concept, critical care, critical illness, intensive care, intensive illness, and serious illness. The search was limited to articles published between 1995 and 2015. The methodological process used in this study was to analyse the literature to identify the content of the concepts critical illness and critical care. The content of each concept was grouped into clusters of related sub-concepts.
Results: The analysis of critical illness identified four clusters: 1) clinical features, 2) aetiology and pathophysiology, 3) diagnostic tests, and 4) prognosis and mortality. The analysis of critical care identified three clusters: 1) the critical care environment, 2) the care provided, and 3) the patient population.
Conclusion: This study provides a framework for the more consistent use of the terms critical illness and critical care. It is anticipated that this will assist in reducing confusion for clinicians and researchers. In addition, the study provides a basis for further research into the concepts critical illness and critical care.
Keywords: critical care; critical illness; concept analysis.

samples.hyp:
The study has several strengths. First, it is the first study to examine the association between long-term exposure to ambient air pollution and the risk of incident dementia in a large national cohort. Second, we used high-resolution air pollution data from a high-resolution chemical transport model, which allowed us to estimate individual-level long-term exposure with reasonable accuracy. Third, we used multiple sources of exposure data and conducted sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of our findings. Fourth, we adjusted for several potential confounding factors, including individual-level socioeconomic status, vascular disease, depression, and sleep disturbance. Finally, the NHA utilized a two-stage random sampling method, which reduced selection bias and increased the representativeness of the sample.
The study also has several limitations. First, we used geospatial interpolation to estimate long-term exposure to air pollution, which may have introduced some exposure misclassification. However, we used a high-resolution chemical transport model to estimate exposure, which has been shown to be more accurate than other methods, such as land use regression models. Second, we did not have information on all potential confounding factors, such as physical activity, cognitive reserve, and genetic factors. Third, we used incident dementia as the outcome, which may have included different subtypes of dementia, such as Alzheimer’s disease and vascular dementia. However, these subtypes have similar risk factors and pathophysiological mechanisms, so this limitation may not have affected our results. Fourth, we did not have information on the duration and severity of dementia, which may have influenced the prognosis and treatment of the disease. Fifth, the NHA is a population-based cohort, which means that it may not include individuals with certain characteristics, such as those with severe dementia or those who were institutionalized. Sixth, the NHA is a large-scale study, which means that it may not have enough power to detect small effects or interactions between air pollution and other risk factors. Finally, the NHA is a retrospective study, which means that it may have some recall bias or measurement error in self-reported data.
In conclusion, our study suggests that long-term exposure to ambient air pollution is associated with an increased risk of dementia in a dose-response manner. The associations were particularly strong for PM2.5 and black carbon, which are markers of traffic-related air pollution. samples.hyp:
The “knocked out” cells were genetically engineered to lack a protein called ASGR1.
The ASGR1 protein is a receptor that helps the liver remove old LDL cholesterol from the blood.
LDL cholesterol is often called “bad cholesterol.”
Previous research had shown that knocking out ASGR1 in mice increased their risk of severe malaria.
The new study found that the ASGR1-deficient liver cells were more likely to be infected with malaria.
The protein on the outside of the malaria parasite binds to ASGR1 on liver cells.
This helps the parasite get inside the liver cell, where it can multiply.
The researchers also found that a drug called obeticholic acid prevented the malaria parasite from binding to ASGR1.
The drug is already approved to treat primary biliary cholangitis, a liver disease.
It is not yet known if the drug would be safe or effective for use in people with malaria.
The study was funded by the Wellcome Trust, the UK Medical Research Council, and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

samples.hyp: Malaria is a mosquito-borne infectious disease caused by the Plasmodium parasite. It is spread to humans through the bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. There are around 40 species of Plasmodium, but the most important are Plasmodium falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, and P. knowlesi. P. falciparum is the most deadly of the five species, causing the majority of malaria-related deaths. The disease is endemic in tropical and subtropical regions, with the highest burden in sub-Saharan Africa. Despite significant progress in reducing malaria cases and deaths in recent years, the disease remains a major public health challenge, particularly in low-income countries. Preventive measures include the use of insecticide-treated bed nets, indoor residual spraying, and antimalarial medications. Early diagnosis and prompt treatment are also crucial in reducing the impact of the disease. However, challenges such as drug resistance, insecticide resistance, and limited access to healthcare services continue to hinder efforts to control and eliminate malaria. Research and development of new tools and strategies are ongoing to address these challenges and achieve the goal of malaria elimination. In conclusion, while significant progress has been made in the fight against malaria, continued efforts are needed to address the remaining challenges and achieve the goal of malaria elimination. This includes increased investment in research and development, improved access to healthcare services, and sustained political commitment to malaria control and elimination efforts. The study aimed to determine the effect of thinning on soil organic matter (SOM) in a 12-year-old Sitka spruce plantation in Ireland. The research was conducted in a plantation located in County Wicklow, Ireland, which had been established in 2006. The plantation was divided into two blocks, each containing four thinning treatments: unthinned control, light thinning, moderate thinning, and heavy thinning. The thinning treatments were applied at the age of 6, 9, and 12 years, with a total of 12 plots per treatment. Soil samples were collected from each plot at a depth of 0-10 cm, and the organic matter content was determined using loss on ignition (LOI) method. The results showed that thinning had a significant effect on SOM content, with the unthinned control having the highest SOM content, followed by the light thinning, moderate thinning, and heavy thinning treatments. The heavy thinning treatment had the lowest SOM content. The canonical correspondence analysis (CCA) revealed that the most significant environmental factors influencing SOM were woodland thinning by clearance, and silt content within soils. Enhancing Chickpea Production and Productivity Through Stakeholders’ Innovation Platform Approach in Ethiopia

Chickpea (Cicer arietinum L.) is an important legume crop in Ethiopia. It is cultivated on 700 thousand hectares with an average productivity of 10.5 q/ha. The crop is mainly grown in semi-arid areas where smallholder farmers are striving to balance the competing demands for food, feed and cash crop production. Chickpea is a key crop for smallholder farmers in Ethiopia. It is cultivated on 700 thousand hectares with an average productivity of 10.5 q/ha. Ethiopia is the second largest producer of chickpea in the world after India. The country produces 35% of the global chickpea production. The crop is also an important foreign exchange earner through export. However, the current productivity level is far below the potential yield estimated by on-station productivity experiments (2.5-2.8 t/ha) and farmers’ field (1.2-1.8 t/ha). Low productivity is mainly due to the adoption of improved varieties (60%), appropriate plant population (60%) and nutrient management (55%) by farmers. The national average productivity of chickpea has not increased significantly in the last two decades. The productivity of chickpea is very low in drought prone areas where the crop is predominantly grown. The low productivity of chickpea is a major concern for smallholder farmers as it limits their income and food security. Therefore, there is a need to increase the productivity of chickpea to improve the livelihood of smallholder farmers. The overall objective of the project is to enhance chickpea production and productivity through stakeholders’ innovation platform approach in Ethiopia. The project will be implemented in collaboration with the Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research (EIAR), non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and chickpea farmers. How Ethiopia boosted chickpea production
10.09.2019
08.00 (CET)
By
Ethiopia has increased its chickpea production by 100% in just three years, thanks to a national breeding programme, according to the country’s top agricultural research official.
Interviewed as part of Crop Science 2019, the biennial conference of the European Society of Agronomy, Dr Muluken Tulu, National Agricultural Research and Training Organisation (NARO) Deputy Director General, said the programme had also increased yields by 20%.
“Chickpea is one of the most important crops in Ethiopia,” he said. “It is a strategic crop for the country, providing food security and foreign exchange.”
Chickpeas are Ethiopia’s fourth most valuable export, after coffee, hides and skins, and spices, according to the World Bank. In 2017, they brought in $500 million.
NARO’s breeding programme focuses on developing varieties that are high yielding, early maturing, and resistant to biotic and abiotic stresses, Dr Tulu said.
“Chickpeas are a cool-season legume that is grown in semi-arid areas, so heat and drought are the main abiotic stresses,” he said. “Biotic stresses are mainly diseases, such as Ascochyta blight and Fusarium wilt, and pests, such as the alfalfa weevil and the pod borer.”
Dr Tulu said the programme had succeeded in developing varieties resistant to Ascochyta blight, the most devastating disease.
NARO has a network of 13 breeding stations across Ethiopia, Dr Tulu said. Varieties are developed there, then multiplied at seed production sites before being distributed to farmers.
“Adoption of new varieties by farmers is very high,” he said. “It is above 90%.”
Dr Tulu said the chickpea breeding programme had been particularly successful because the organisation had invested in capacity building.
“We have a large number of breeders,” he said. “We have 42 in total.”
Dr Tulu said NARO was now working on a new chickpea breeding strategy.
“We are revising our national chickpea breeding strategy,” he said. “We are planning to introduce marker-assisted selection into our breeding programme.”

The present study was designed to investigate the testicular toxicity of sodium metavanadate (NaVO3) in adult male African giant rats (Cricetomys gambianus). The animals were orally administered with different concentrations (0.5, 1.0, and 1.5 mg/kg body weight) of NaVO3 for 30 consecutive days. At the end of the experiment, the animals were sacrificed and testes removed for histological and ultrastructural analyses. The results showed a significant (P < 0.05) reduction in body weight, testis weight, and absolute and relative testis weights. The histoarchitecture of the seminiferous tubules was also significantly (P < 0.05) altered with varying degrees of degeneration, vacuolations, germinal epithelium lifting, and germ cell depletion. The epidymides were also unable to support spermiation. The epididymal fluid analysis showed a significant (P < 0.05) reduction in sperm count, viability, and motility. The present study was conducted in Begi Woreda, West Wellega Zone, West Shewa, West Ethiopia to document the indigenous knowledge of homegarden plants. A total of 104 homegarden holders were interviewed using semi-structured interviews. The results showed that the homegarden holders have rich knowledge on the use of homegarden plants. They used 102 plant species from 30 families for different purposes. The families with the highest number of plant contributors were Asteraceae (14), Poaceae (12), Euphorbiaceae (8), Fabaceae (7), Solanaceae (6), and Rubiaceae (5). samples.hyp:
Homegardens are a common agroforestry system in tropical mountainous regions. They are multi-storeyed, managed systems, which provide a variety of food and non-food products to their owners. In this study, floristic composition, diversity and similarity of homegardens were studied in the Gozamin district of Northwest Ethiopia. A total of 20 homegardens, ten from the Wole-raa and ten from the Begi-woreda district, were selected randomly. The selected homegardens were 1-25 years old, and ranged in size from 100 to 1000 m2. A belt transect of 10 m × 10 m was used to record all plant species in each homegarden. Data on species identity, life form, origin, growth habit, and number of individuals per species were collected. A total of 176 species belonging to 86 genera and 45 families were recorded. The most species-rich families were Rubiaceae, Euphorbiaceae, Verbenaceae, Solanaceae, and Vitaceae. Exotic species accounted for 34% of the total number of species, 38% of the total number of individuals, and 43% of the total basal cover. The highest diversity (H' = 2.62) was found in the Wole-raa homegardens, while the lowest diversity (H' = 1.48) was found in the Begi-woreda homegardens. The highest similarity (S = 72.5%) was found between the 11-year-old and the 18-year-old homegardens. The floristic composition of homegardens in Northwest Ethiopia in general, and the Gozamin district in particular, has received little research attention. More research is needed to understand the floristic composition, diversity, and similarity of homegardens in Ethiopia.

Their results showed that the community used plants for food, medicine, building, fodder (animal feed), and other cultural uses.
Results
The informants identified 100 plant species in the study area. The informants were knowledgeable about the uses of the plants, and the uses reported by the informants are listed in Table 1. The informants reported that 77% of the species were used for food, 68% for building, 66% for medicine, 52% for fodder, 13% for crafts, 12% for ceremonies, 11% for fuel, and 4% for poison. The informants reported 14 different parts of the plants were used, including the fruit (39 species), leaves (36 species), root (33 species), stem (29 species), whole plant (26 species), bark (22 species), flower (19 species), seed (16 species), wood (14 species), rhizome (12 species), fruit shoot (11 species), young leaves (10 species), inflorescence (9 species), and young stem (8 species). The bark of the plants was used for 36 purposes, the leaves for 32 purposes, the root for 28 purposes, the fruit for 23 purposes, the wood for 16 purposes, the whole plant for 14 purposes, the seed for 10 purposes, the fruit shoot for 9 purposes, the stem for 7 purposes, the young leaves for 5 purposes, the rhizome for 4 purposes, and the inflorescence for 3 purposes.
Food
The informants reported that 59 species were used as food, including 30 species of fruit, 20 species of root, 12 species of stem, 10 species of leaves, 6 species of flower, and 1 species of seed. The fruits of 21 species were eaten fresh, and the fruits of 9 species were processed. The fresh fruits were eaten by all age groups, and the processed fruits were eaten mainly by adults. The fresh fruits were eaten raw or cooked. The processed fruits were made into juice, jam, or sauce. The leaves of 11 species were eaten fresh, and the leaves of 1 species were processed.
